Headers like Content-Length, Host, Postman-Token, User-Agent, Accept-Encoding and Connection are added by Postman itself ("calculated when request is sent"), so you don't need to maintain them manually.

entry.title: From SOAP to RAP: Choosing a Web Service Technology in S/4HANA
entry.content:
1. Introduction

Over the years, SAP has introduced several generations of web service technology, and anyone starting a new integration project on S/4HANA today can easily lose track of which option actually fits the use case. Should an existing BAPI be released as a SOAP service? Should a classic OData v2 service be built with the Gateway Service Builder? Or is it better to go straight to RAP and OData v4, and if so, which flavor of RAP? This article is a practical, comparison-oriented overview for architects and developers who need to make that call. It is not a deep dive into any of the single technologies.

Scope. To keep the comparison practical, this article is limited to HTTP-based technologies that run entirely inside the S/4HANA system. In other words, it covers options that work without provisioning separate components such as SAP BTP Integration Suite or Event Mesh.

Read vs. write. All example calls are deliberately read-only. This keeps the examples short and comparable across technologies, without the extra complexity of create/update/delete semantics. Every technology section nevertheless explains how write access differs, so the full picture is covered.

Running example. To make the comparison concrete, every section uses the same fictional scenario: retrieving a business partner’s name and address. The data comes from the tables BUT000 (general business partner data), ADRC (address data) and BUT020 (mapping between the two). This is a small join, but a realistic and common one in S/4HANA projects, and complex enough to show how each technology copes with more than a flat, single-table lookup.

A decision matrix at the end of the article compares the technologies across several criteria: future viability, how much of the interface is defined by the developer versus dictated by the respective framework, the degree of manual implementation effort and the technical basis involved.

 

2. SOAP (RFC/BAPI released as a web service)

How it works: This is the most traditional way of exposing web service in S/4 HANA. An existing RFC-enabled function module or BAPI is released via the SOA-Manager, which generates a WSDL from the function module’s signature (import/export parameters, tables etc.). The function module itself is the implementation, so no additional code has to be written.

Implementation: First, an RFC-enabled function module is selected for exposure, either a standard one or a self-written one. A wizard in the Function Builder then creates the service definition. Alternatively, the service definition can be created in the Object Navigator (SE80). In both cases, the service is subsequently configured and activated as a runtime service in the SOA-Manager.

For the running example, this could mean either developing a custom function module that performs the table join, or choosing a standard one such as the BAPI BAPI_BUPA_ADDRESS_GETDETAIL.

Example call: Unlike the REST-style URLs discussed below, the endpoint of a SOAP service can contain multiple operations. The operation to be called is specified inside the XML body. A fictional endpoint might look like this:

POST https://<system>.example.com:44300/sap/bc/srt/rfc/sap/z_bp_address_read/300/z_bp_address_read/z_bp_address_read

Content-Type: text/xml; charset=utf-8

The HTTP request body wraps the operation and its import parameters in a <soap:Envelope>/<soap:Body> structure. The response mirrors the export parameters and tables back as XML.

Write access: For create/update, a write-enabled function module is released in the same way as a read-only one, for example the BAPIs BAPI_BUPA_CREATE and BAPI_BUPA_ADDRESS_ADD. Transaction handling is usually done server-side inside the function module, although client-steered commit handling is possible as well.

Error handling: Errors can surface on three different levels: Technical failures are reported via the HTTP status code (e.g. 500). SOAP Faults are standardized error structures inside the SOAP envelope, containing a fault code and message, and are usually returned together with HTTP status 500, for example for invalid request XML or an uncaught exception in the function module. Business errors such as “business partner not found” often arrive as a valid response with a RETURN table (e.g. BAPIRET2) and a message type like E, but can also be raised as SOAP Faults. Consumers therefore need to evaluate the HTTP status, the SOAP Fault and the business-level return structure.

Other features: The service’s capabilities are described in a metadata file following the Web Service Description Language (WSDL). Further features, such as switching between XML and JSON, filtering, or paging for high-volume calls, are either not feasible or have to be implemented manually in each function module.

When to use it: SOAP-released BAPIs can mainly be understood as legacy. SAP does not recommend this approach for new development, and hasn’t for some time. It can still be a reasonable choice when a function module already does exactly what is required and no suitable CDS views or standard OData services exist. In most other cases, the strategically recommended path is found in the later sections of this article, particularly RAP with OData v4.

 

3. OData v2 (SAP Gateway / SEGW)

How it works: The SAP Gateway Service Builder introduced a structured way of exposing data as a REST-based service following the OData v2 protocol. Entities and their relationships are modelled in transaction SEGW, while the actual data retrieval is implemented manually in generated ABAP classes, typically by redefining methods such as GET_ENTITYSET or GET_ENTITY. The resulting service follows OData v2 conventions for addressing, filtering and other query options.

Implementation: The typical path starts with creating a project in the Service Builder (SEGW), where the entity types and entity sets are defined. In the running example these would be BusinessPartner and BusinessPartnerAddress, including their relationship. After generating the development artifacts, the data provider class is implemented, for example by calling a suitable read BAPI or by selecting directly from the underlying tables or views inside GET_ENTITYSET. Finally, the service is activated and registered in /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE, which makes it callable.

Example call: OData’s URL conventions make reading a specific business partner and its address look like this:

GET https://<system>.example.com/sap/opu/odata/sap/ZBP_ADDRESS_V2/BusinessPartnerAddressSet('P1001')?$expand=_toAddress

Accept: application/json

Since this is a GET call, no HTTP body is required for read access.

Error handling: Errors come back as standard HTTP status codes (404 for a business partner that doesn’t exist, 400 for a malformed filter, and so on), together with an OData-standard JSON or XML error message in the HTTP body containing an error message and an error code.

Write access: Create, update and delete operations map to the standard HTTP verbs (POST, PUT, DELETE) against the entity set. They are implemented by redefining the corresponding methods (CREATE_ENTITY, UPDATE_ENTITY, DELETE_ENTITY) in the same data provider class. The content of the respective data set is sent in the HTTP body.

Other features: OData v2 comes with built-in query options such as filtering on specific fields, selecting data by key or regular fields, and paging. In SEGW, however, most of these must be implemented manually in the data provider classes. On the output side, both XML and JSON are supported, with JSON being the de facto default in most implementations today. OData v2 also provides a service description in the form of an EDMX file following the Common Schema Definition Language (CSDL), which can be retrieved by appending $metadata to the service root.

When to use it: OData v2 via SEGW is stable, and many systems rely on it, but it is no longer where SAP’s strategic development effort goes. For new services, SAP steers toward RAP. Note that RAP can also expose services via OData v2, so "OData v2" and "SEGW" are not strictly the same decision.

 

4. Custom REST (ICF handler)

How it works: This option builds on a rather basic framework: a handler class is registered directly in the Internet Communication Framework (SICF). The handler class acts as a dispatcher. It interprets incoming calls and selects and executes a suitable resource class. There is no metadata, no generated create/read/update/delete (CRUD) functionality and no standardized query syntax. The developer decides on the URL structure, the payload shape, the HTTP verbs used, and how (or whether) to support filtering and paging, down to the interpretation and setting of each individual HTTP header. This makes it the most flexible option covered here, and also the one with the least built-in support.

Implementation: The starting point is a handler class implementing the interface IF_HTTP_EXTENSION. This class interprets the service-specific part of the URI and matches it against registered patterns, similar to regular expressions. When the URI matches a pattern, the resource class registered for that pattern is called. Patterns can contain variables, for instance /client/{clientid: [1-9][0-9]*}. A call ending in /client/4711 would invoke the registered resource class with the parameter clientid set to 4711.

The resource class must implement the interface IF_REST_RESOURCE, in which the methods for the individual HTTP verbs can be redefined (e.g. IF_REST_RESOURCE~GET). Inside these methods, the variables from the URI are available, as well as other inputs such as HTTP headers, the HTTP body and query parameters. After parsing these, the business logic is executed, and the HTTP status code, response headers and response body are set by the custom code.

Example call: Since there is no protocol convention to follow, the shape is entirely up to the developer. A call might look like this:

GET https://<system>.example.com/sap/bc/zbp_address/Partner/P1001

Accept: application/json

Error handling: Also entirely custom: the development team decides which HTTP status codes to return and how to structure the error body.

Write access: No different in principle from read access. The development team handles the HTTP verbs and payload parsing, and is fully responsible for locking, transactional consistency and validation, since none of the generic RAP or Gateway services apply here.

Other features: Features such as filtering or paging must be implemented from scratch. The response format is entirely free (JSON, XML or anything else). The response body is serialized manually, for JSON for example often with the class /ui2/cl_json.

When to use it: This option is most sensible when a use case genuinely doesn’t fit the standard interfaces, for example because of a highly custom payload shape, a non-CRUD-style API, or a need for tight control over the exact response format. It comes, however, at the price of conceptualizing and implementing a lot of different features that come for free elsewhere.

 

5. RAP (ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model) / OData v4

RAP is SAP’s current strategic model for building services, and the one most closely tied to the Clean Core principle in S/4HANA and to ABAP Cloud. Rather than a single technology, RAP is better understood as a framework with one standard implementation style (managed) and two custom implementation styles (custom entity and unmanaged). These styles differ substantially in how much the framework does and how much has to be implemented by hand. All three are introduced together here because they share the same tooling and core concepts.

5.1 Standard (managed) RAP

How it works: This is the standard way of developing in RAP. Core Data Services (CDS) view entities are defined and connected, and a behavior definition marked as managed is added on top. The framework then generates features such as CRUD from declarative annotations, so no read, create or update methods have to be written by hand.

Implementation: The foundation is a virtual data model made up of CDS views along two dimensions. The first dimension consists of three layers of views defined by SAP: basic views, composite views and consumption views. The second dimension is the relationships between the business entities in those views. In the running example, three basic views are created to access the tables BUT000, BUT020 and ADRC. On the interface layer, two views are created: Z_I_PARTNER and Z_I_PARTNER_ADDRESS. The first reads from the BUT000 basic view, while the second joins the data from BUT020 and ADRC. The two interface views are linked by a composition reflecting the parent-child relationship between partner and address. To expose the model, two consumption views are created which are based on the interface views and restrict the exposed fields to only the one’s necessary in the interface. Next, a behavior definition turns the entity model into a business object (BO) by annotating it with a set of keywords describing its features (see below). Finally, a service definition exposes the relevant entities, and a service binding (UI or Web API, OData v2 or v4) makes the service callable from outside. Note that the whole implementation can be done without writing any ABAP code: only CDS views and configuration artifacts are created. However, adding operations on top of CRUD is possible as determinations and actions using ABAP.

Example call: The shape of read access depends on whether OData v2 or v4 is chosen in the service binding. An OData v4 example could look like this:

GET https://<system>.example.com/sap/opu/odata4/sap/zsb_address_v4/srvd/sap/zsd_address/0001/BusinessPartnerAddress('P1001')

Accept: application/json

Error handling: As with SEGW, errors come back as standard HTTP status codes, accompanied by an OData-standard message in the HTTP body containing an error message and an error code.

Write access: Write capabilities are added declaratively through annotations in the behavior definition. This covers create, update and delete, as well as transaction handling and the ability to save draft versions.

Other features: Standard RAP comes with a wide range of built-in features, which are either active by default or can be added via annotations in the behavior definition. Some of them are: (1) paging, including the use of a skip token, (2) automatic generation of key values for new entries, (3) lock handling for concurrent write processes, (4) authorization handling on different levels, (5) automatic switching between XML and JSON response formats (for OData v2).

When to use it: This is the technology SAP actively recommends for new S/4HANA development, and the one best aligned with Clean Core extensibility. If one is starting from scratch and the interface required is about exposing data consisting of different linked entities based on database tables (as opposed to interfaces with rather algorithmic nature), this is the default choice. It does require a change in thinking about interfaces: Instead of one endpoint for each part or angle of the data in a traditional input-output setup, a data model for a whole domain can be exposed. If that model is well structured, many different data needs can be fulfilled simply through the right OData parameters of one interface endpoint. Parameterizing the requests can be a challenge of it’s own, though, because deciding which entities to read, with which fields, in which order and for which filter criteria, can get very complex.

5.2 RAP with custom entity

How it works: Sometimes data doesn’t come from a straightforward CDS view over a database table. It might come from an RFC call to another system, from a computed result, or from a BAPI wrapping complex logic. A custom entity keeps the consistency of RAP and OData (same tooling, same protocol, same annotation model) while the data retrieval is implemented by hand.

Implementation: The entity’s attributes are defined in a custom-entity CDS definition, marked with the annotation @ObjectModel.query.implementedBy, which names a custom ABAP class. Note that, unlike regular CDS views, a custom entity does not rely on a database table or another view. The ABAP class implements the interface IF_RAP_QUERY_PROVIDER. The signature of its method provides all OData parameters sent by the caller, so it is the developer's duty to handle these parameters and to retrieve and return the result data. The custom entity is then exposed through a behavior definition (in this case optional), a service definition and a service binding, just as with standard entities.

Comparison with standard RAP: With a custom entity, the RAP framework still receives and parses the call’s parameters, but reacting to them is up to the developer’s own ABAP logic. Most OData features therefore remain available in principle, but most of them must be programmed manually. This is also why mixing custom and standard entities within a complex virtual data model can be very challenging and is in some cases impossible. A second limitation is that managed custom entities are read-only. For custom RAP developments with write access, unmanaged business objects are the right choice.

When to use it: A useful complement to standard RAP for read-only scenarios in which standard RAP cannot be used. Where possible, however, prefer exposing the full data model over single, isolated custom entities.

5.3 Unmanaged RAP

How it works: This style provides full control over a business object, including all write operations. The data model can be defined with regular CDS views or custom entities. In contrast to managed RAP, however, the transactional behavior (create, update, delete, locking, authorization and saving) is not generated by the framework but implemented manually.

Implementation: The data model is built from regular CDS views or custom entities just as in managed RAP. In the behavior definition, the business object is then marked as unmanaged together with the name of an implementation class. This class contains local classes: one inheriting from CL_ABAP_BEHAVIOR_HANDLER, in which the methods for creating, updating, deleting, locking and authorizations are implemented, and a second one inheriting from CL_ABAP_BEHAVIOR_SAVER, which gives full control over the LUW transaction handling and the actual saving of the data.

Comparison with standard RAP: Compared to standard RAP or custom entities, unmanaged business objects offer the maximum control over functionality, at the cost of considerably more implementation effort. In this respect they are roughly comparable to the custom REST approach described above. The difference is that a custom REST handler is a very loose framework in which almost everything is a free decision, whereas unmanaged business objects come with a much stricter framework. That framework can act as a guardrail for the implementation, but it can also mean implementing functionality the project does not actually need.

Where this stands today: Valid and supported, but with meaningfully more implementation effort than managed RAP. It should be a deliberate choice for cases that need the control, not a default.

 

6 Decision matrix

The matrix below summarizes technical aspects of the technologies as well as the author’s rating on several dimensions. It lists custom entities and unmanaged business objects as separate rows, since their characteristics genuinely diverge from standard RAP.

 

TechnologyImplementation baseMetadata fileStandard/ProtocolRead / Write  possibleError handlingModernizationFlexibilityFramework SupportManual implementation efforts
SOAP with SOAMANAGERABAPWSDLSOAPRead / WriteSemi-standardizedLowHighLowHigh
Odata with SEGWABAPCSDL/EDMXOdata v2Read / WriteStandardizedLowLowMediumHigh
Custom RESTABAPNoneNoneRead / WriteCustomLowHighLowHigh
Standard RAPCDS ViewsCSDL/EDMXOdata v2 / v4Read / WriteStandardizedHighLowHighLow
RAP with custom entitiesCDS Views + ABAPCSDL/EDMXOdata v2 / v4Read onlyStandardizedHighMediumMediumHigh
RAP with unmanaged BOCDS Views + ABAPCSDL/EDMXOdata v2 / v4Read / WriteStandardizedHighMediumMediumHigh

Technical aspects. Implementation base names the languages or artifact types mainly used for the implementation. Metadata file is the machine-readable service description offered by the technology. Standard / protocol is the protocol the service follows. Read / write shows whether the technology supports write operations. Error handling indicates how standardized error handling is supported beyond plain HTTP status codes.

Ratings. Modernity refers to the roadmap communicated by SAP. Flexibility describes the freedom an implementation offers within the technology. Framework support describes how much the framework does for the developer. Manual effort describes how much has to be implemented by hand. The ratings are subjective, as they would be for any other author, and are meant as broad tendencies only. Their values depend on the individual use case. If a function module already exists that does exactly what is required, the implementation effort with SOAP is naturally very low. Conversely, the effort with standard RAP can be high if the required functionality does not fit well into a CRUD and OData scheme. The same applies to flexibility. Unmanaged business objects are rated medium because, despite their manual implementation, the RAP framework still prescribes much more structure than, for example, a custom REST handler.

 

7. Conclusion

The comparison shows that the further one moves from SOAP or Custom REST toward managed RAP, the more the framework takes over and the less control (and boilerplate code) remains for the developer. This reflects the typical trade-off between flexibility and framework support that is inherent in virtually every programming framework.

In line with SAP’s recommendation, RAP, and in particular standard (managed) RAP, should be the strategic default for new, Clean-Core-aligned services on S/4HANA. It is also the area into which SAP directs its tooling and documentation efforts. The other technologies nevertheless remain relevant in specific situations. SOAP-released BAPIs are the fastest way to expose functionality that already exists as a function module, and given their widespread use in existing landscapes, it is unlikely that they will disappear simply because SAP no longer recommends them. OData v2 via SEGW is a reasonable choice when extending an existing Gateway-based landscape. Finally, a custom REST service based on an ICF handler remains an option for requirements that fit no standardized model at all. It trades standardization, such as metadata, paging and error conventions, for flexibility, and this trade-off should be a deliberate decision.

Within RAP, standard RAP, custom entity and unmanaged business objects are not competing alternatives but tools for different situations. Standard RAP is best suited to exposing an entire data model of several interconnected entities with few or no algorithmic requirements. A custom entity is appropriate when the data cannot easily be derived from CDS views over database tables and only needs to be read. An unmanaged business object keeps the CDS-based model but replaces the generated transactional behavior with custom logic. It therefore fits cases in which write operations do not match the generated CRUD model, for example when they involve many case distinctions or the reuse of existing function modules. In each case, the choice follows the same principle: the more of the implementation is taken over by custom logic, the more control is gained, and the more of the framework’s support is given up.

entry.title: Calling SAP SuccessFactors from Postman with OAuth 2.0 (SAML Bearer Assertion) - No External Tools
entry.content:
SAP SuccessFactors is retiring HTTP Basic Authentication (user and password) for its APIs. The retirement is planned for November 2026, and published sources give either 13 or 20 November, so the earlier date is the safer one to plan for. After that date, OData calls and SOAP calls such as CompoundEmployee will only accept token-based authentication.

If you use SAP Integration Suite (CPI), the switch is mostly a matter of configuration: you create an OAuth2 SAML Bearer Assertion credential and the adapter handles the rest. Manual testing in Postman has no equivalent built-in support. This post explains how to reproduce, step by step, what CPI does internally, using only Postman and OpenSSL.

The complete Postman collection, with all scripts in English, is attached to this post.

What you will be able to do

  • Generate your own RSA key pair and X.509 certificate.
  • Register an OAuth 2.0 client application in SAP SuccessFactors.
  • Build and digitally sign a SAML 2.0 assertion inside Postman, without any external tool.
  • Exchange the assertion for an OAuth access token and call the OData API.
  • Open an SFAPI session with the token and query CompoundEmployee over SOAP.

No prior OAuth or SAML knowledge is assumed. The explanations cover what happens at each step and why.

How it works

The method is the OAuth 2.0 SAML Bearer Assertion grant. Instead of sending a password, you send SuccessFactors a short XML document, the assertion. The assertion states that the application with a given API Key is acting as a given user and that the request is valid for the next 10 minutes. You sign the assertion with a private key. SuccessFactors verifies the signature with the public certificate you registered earlier. If the signature matches, it returns an access token valid for about 24 hours, and you attach that token to every API call.

The setup has two parts:

  1. One-time setup: create a technical user with the right permissions, generate a key pair, register the certificate in an OAuth client in SuccessFactors, and create a Postman environment.
  2. Every session: generate the assertion, get the token, then call the OData API or open an SFAPI session and query CompoundEmployee.

Step A: Technical user and permissions

Create or reuse a dedicated technical user, for example API_TECH_USER, and assign a permission role that includes:

  • Employee Central API → Employee Central HRIS OData API and Foundation OData API, for access to Employee Central entities.
  • Employee Central API → Employee Central HRIS SOAP API, required for CompoundEmployee.
  • General User Permission → SFAPI User Login, required to open an SFAPI session.
  • The target population and field-level RBP. These define which employees and fields the API returns. If they are too narrow, you get empty results.

The permission Allow Admin to Access OData API through Basic Authentication is not needed for OAuth. Once the migration is complete, you can remove it to verify that nothing still depends on Basic Authentication.

Step B: Key pair and certificate

Generate a self-signed certificate and private key with OpenSSL:

openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -sha256 -days 36500 -nodes \
  -keyout private.pem -out cert.pem -subj "/CN=postman-sf-ACMECORPT1"

Key points:

  • -nodes leaves the private key unencrypted. The Postman script needs an unencrypted PKCS#8 key.
  • The validity period is a decision to make together with the customer, in line with their security policy. A long validity avoids renewing the certificate and updating every Postman environment each year. A shorter lifetime reduces the impact if the key leaks. Either way, record the expiry date with openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -enddate.

SuccessFactors and the Postman variables need the Base64 content without the BEGIN/END lines and without line breaks. On Linux, macOS or Git Bash:

grep -v -- "-----" private.pem | tr -d '\n' > private_b64.txt
grep -v -- "-----" cert.pem    | tr -d '\n' > cert_b64.txt

On Windows PowerShell, use the equivalent Get-Content, Where-Object and Set-Content commands. The public certificate goes to SuccessFactors and to the Postman variable certificate_b64. The private key goes only into the Postman variable private_key_b64, and it must never be shared.

Step C: Register the OAuth client in SuccessFactors

In Admin Center, open Manage OAuth2 Client Applications and choose Register Client Application. Fill in:

  • Company: the tenant company ID (prefilled).
  • Application Name: free text. It appears in the token as issuedFor.
  • Application URL: used for identification only. No call is made to it.
  • Bind to Users: checked, and the technical user ID added. This restricts token issuance to the listed users and is recommended.
  • X.509 Certificate: paste the single-line Base64 certificate.

Do not click Generate X.509 Certificate. That creates a different key pair, and you already have yours. After registering, open the client and copy the API Key. It becomes the Postman variable client_id. The API Key is not a secret on its own, but it cannot be used to obtain tokens without the private key.

Step Postman environment

Create an environment, for example SF ACME Preview, with these variables:

Variable Content

urlThe API server of your data center, without a trailing slash. This is not the UI URL. Find it in SAP's list of SuccessFactors API servers.
userThe technical user ID from Step A. It goes into the assertion NameID.
companyThe tenant company ID.
client_idThe API Key of the OAuth client.
private_key_b64Content of private_b64.txt. Set the type to secret and fill only the Current value.
certificate_b64Content of cert_b64.txt. Optional, added to the assertion KeyInfo.
assertion, assertion_xml, sf_token, sf_token_exp, sessionIdLeft empty. They are written by the requests.

Postman keeps an Initial value and a Current value for each variable. Keep the private key, tokens and assertions in the Current value only, so they are not synced to the workspace or included in exports.

Collection structure

The collection can be run from top to bottom with the Collection Runner, or one request at a time:

  • SF SAML Bearer step by step
    1. Generate assertion: downloads the jsrsasign library and builds the signed assertion.
    2. Get token: exchanges the assertion for an access token.
    3. Call OData resource: calls the OData API with the Bearer token.
  • CompoundEmployee
    • Login CE: opens the SFAPI session.
    • GET CompoundEmployee: runs the SOAP query.
  • AllInOneCall (optional): a pre-request script that obtains a token automatically when needed.

Request 1: Generating the SAML assertion

SuccessFactors does not create the assertion for you. The old /oauth/idp endpoint is deprecated, because it required sending the private key over the network. So the assertion has to be built and signed on the client side. Postman's sandbox includes CryptoJS for hashing but no RSA signing, so the script first downloads jsrsasign, a pure JavaScript cryptography library.

The assertion contains:

  • ID and IssueInstant: a random identifier and the current UTC time.
  • Issuer: the fixed value www.successfactors.com.
  • Signature: an enveloped XML signature, placed right after the Issuer.
  • Subject / NameID: the technical user the API calls will run as.
  • SubjectConfirmationData: the Recipient is the /oauth/token endpoint.
  • Conditions: a validity window from 5 minutes in the past to 10 minutes in the future.
  • AttributeStatement: an api_key attribute with the client ID, which tells SuccessFactors which registered certificate to use.

The signature is produced in three steps. First, the assertion without the signature is hashed with SHA-256. Second, a small SignedInfo block describing the algorithms and the digest is assembled. Third, SignedInfo is signed with the private key using RSA-SHA256. SuccessFactors repeats the same computation with the registered certificate. If one byte differs, the verification fails.

One detail matters a lot: XML signatures are computed over a canonical form of the XML (Exclusive XML Canonicalization, exc-c14n). Postman has no canonicalization library, so the script writes the XML already in canonical form, with no spaces or line breaks between elements, attributes in alphabetical order and explicit closing tags. Do not reformat or indent the XML parts of the script. A single extra space breaks the signature.

Request 2: Getting the access token

The assertion is exchanged at {{url}}/oauth/token as an x-www-form-urlencoded body with four fields: client_id, company_id, grant_type set to urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:saml2-bearer, and assertion. This must happen within the 10-minute window of the assertion.

The post-response script stores sf_token and an expiry timestamp. The expiry is set 5 minutes early to avoid using a token that expires in the middle of a call.

The token is Base64-encoded JSON. Decoding it is a useful sanity check, because it shows which API key and which user it was issued for.

Request 3: Calling the OData API

With the token, OData calls are simple: the token goes in the Authorization: Bearer header. For example:

  • GET {{url}}/odata/v2/User?$top=5&$format=json
  • GET {{url}}/odata/v2/PerPerson?$top=5&$format=json
  • GET {{url}}/odata/v2/EmpJob?$filter=userId eq '100001'&$select=userId,startDate,company,department,jobCode&$format=json

To check whether a token is still valid, call {{url}}/oauth/validate with the Bearer token.

CompoundEmployee via SFAPI

CompoundEmployee is exposed by the SFAPI, the older SOAP API. Unlike OData, SFAPI works with sessions. A login operation returns a session ID, which is also set as the JSESSIONID cookie, and every query must carry that session.

The key finding from testing: sending the Bearer token directly on the query returns INVALID_SESSION. The token must first be used in a login call, and the login body must have empty companyId, username and password elements. If companyId or username are filled in, SuccessFactors attempts a classic password login and fails with FAILED_AUTHENTICATION. If the password element is removed altogether, the request fails schema validation. So the working combination is empty elements plus the Bearer header, which returns a session ID.

Then, for the query:

  • Set the cookie explicitly: Cookie: JSESSIONID={{sessionId}}.
  • Disable the Postman cookie jar, so that old session cookies are not sent.
  • Use a SOAP query with a SELECT on CompoundEmployee, for example on person, personal_information, employment_information and job_information.
  • For incremental extracts, add a delta filter such as WHERE last_modified_on > to_datetime('...'). Inside XML, the greater-than sign must be written as >.
  • When the response contains <hasMore>true</hasMore>, call queryMore with the returned querySessionId until hasMore is false.

The SFAPI session expires after 10 minutes of inactivity. If you get INVALID_SESSION, run the login again.

Lifetimes and run order

Item Lifetime When to regenerate

SAML assertion10 minutesRun Request 1 again if Request 2 is sent later than that.
Access tokenAbout 24 hoursRun Requests 1 and 2 again. The step-by-step flow does not refresh automatically.
SFAPI session10 minutes of inactivityRun Login CE again on INVALID_SESSION.
CertificateAs generated, or as agreed with the customerRotate before expiry: new key pair, then update the OAuth client and the Postman variables together.

A typical session is: generate the assertion, get the token, call OData as needed, log in to SFAPI, then run the CompoundEmployee query.

Troubleshooting

A few of the errors encountered while building this setup:

  • Identifier 't' has already been declared: the library was loaded in the same scope as the script. Load it with new Function(...), as the script does.
  • getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND undefined: a variable does not exist in the selected environment. Check the variable names and that the environment is selected.
  • Error from KEYUTIL.getKey: the key is not PKCS#8 or it is truncated. Regenerate it with -nodes, and check that the first line is -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----.
  • /oauth/token rejects the assertion: the certificate registered in SuccessFactors does not match the key, the XML was altered, the clocks are out of sync, or the assertion is older than 10 minutes.
  • INVALID_SESSION on SOAP calls: the query was sent with the Bearer token instead of the session cookie, or an old cookie was sent. Log in first and disable the cookie jar.
  • FAILED_AUTHENTICATION on login: the credential elements were not empty, or the Bearer header was not set on the request.

Security

  • The private key is equivalent to the credentials of the technical user. Keep it only in the Postman Current value, marked as secret. Never commit it to a repository or share it in chats. Ideally, each colleague generates their own key pair and OAuth client.
  • Never send tokens to third-party hosts. The request that downloads the library from cdnjs must use No Auth. An inherited Bearer token would be sent to that host.
  • Use a dedicated technical user with minimal permissions and a restricted target population, and enable Bind to Users on the OAuth client.
  • Use separate key pairs and OAuth clients for each tenant, for example preview and production.
  • Once OAuth works, remove the Basic Authentication permission from the technical user.

Attached material

The attached Postman collection, OAuth Assertion - SuccessFactors, contains all the requests described above, in the order they should run, the complete Request 1 script, and the optional AllInOneCall request, which handles token renewal automatically.

Note: SAP Community does not accept .json attachments, so the collection is provided as a .txt file. Rename it to OAuth_Assertion_SuccessFactors.postman_collection.json before importing it into Postman. The file content is unchanged.

Before importing it, create the environment described in Step D. The collection contains no secrets. All tenant data in the examples (URLs, company ID, user, API key, keys and IDs) are fictitious, so replace them with your own tenant values.

I hope this helps anyone who needs to test SuccessFactors APIs from Postman without Basic Authentication. Questions and feedback are welcome in the comments

entry.title: ABAP to Full Stack: Making Sense of What’s Behind a Fiori App (OData, Class, Virtual Element)
entry.content:
Hello! I’m Andréa Molina. After more than 20 years in SAP, the new SAP world left me completely lost, so I decided to share my experience and learn together. I’m moving from classic ABAP to the SAP full stack, one real project at a time, drama included.

From overwhelmed to curious, my journey had (and still has) a lot of bumps. You can check my other posts here. I hope you find understanding and empathy here, and maybe a few laughs.

If you’re in the same boat, this series is for you. In this post: I will share my experience creating a List Report (a Fiori floorplan) built on a CDS view exposed as OData V4, with a virtual element calculated by an ABAP class. Plus a plot twist in Step 5.

A bit of background

On my journey I always try to use case studies that are real and will add value to the business. The library and ice cream examples just give me more anxiety and make no sense to me. So this time I’m turning an existing query/infoset (SQ01/SQ02) into a Fiori app, to understand how much effort and time it would take.

So far I have worked with the Basic template and one CDS KPI app, and I knew there were more template options to explore. This time I thought the List Report Page would work best (well, not really, but let’s move forward for now... surprise at Step 5 of this blog).

Before we move on, read this if you are asking "What on earth is List Report Page and Basic Template?"
When you create a new app from a template, you can choose among a lot of frameworks. Each framework provides a set of prebuilt files, structure and more.

You can read more about FloorPlans here: https://www.sap.com/design-system/fiori-design-web/v1-136/page-types/floorplans/when-to-use-which-floorplan

The project

Transform an existing Query/InfoSet (SQ01/SQ02) into a Fiori application. 

Does SAP Make This Easy?

In my research and studying I couldn't find a tool that automatically converts queries into Fiori applications. If you know of a better approach, please share it in the comments. I'd genuinely love to learn. 

The Challenge

… because I have never done before this project

  • Create a CDS view that delivers the data exactly the way I want it to be displayed, with logic and not just selection from the database
  • Create an ABAP class that is called by the CDS
  • Understand how the ABAP class and the CDS work together
  • Create a KPI on top of the report list

The best way to learn: get your hands dirty! A simple learning exercise 

I am suggesting here a very simple example of CDS, class and app: create a List Report Page based on a CDS.

The result should show all the Sales Orders created in the last 30 days and flag the ones created today.

Step 0: Eclipse

The way to create backend objects for apps is using the ABAP Development Tools (ADT) in Eclipse. If you are new here, check this tutorial to set up your Eclipse ADT: https://developers.sap.com/tutorials/abap-install-adt/ 

Step 1: The CDS Views

To get familiar with frontend and backend (together, they make the full stack), here is what is what.

  • Backend: where the data comes from.
  • Frontend: the screen the user interacts with. This part of the development is the backend.

What is backend: Where the data comes from. Put in very simple words.  it's the data that will populate the frontend. 

The CDS will select from I_SalesOrder, and we will use a virtual element (calculated by an ABAP class) to flag the orders created today. It will only return the last 30 days, so we don't select hundreds of records. 🥴 

Why I_SalesOrder and not VBAK?

If you grew up in ECC like I did, you might be asking: why not use VBAK?

  • Tables move, CDS adapts. Moving from ECC to S/4HANA changed a lot of tables. Take VBUK, where we used to read the order status. Its fields now live in VBAK, so every program that selected from VBUK needs to change. But a program reading the status through I_SalesOrder will keep working, because SAP updated the view and left the interface alone. That's the idea behind released CDS views: SAP can rearrange it, and your app doesn't notice.
  • Clean core. Clean core is the promise of updating the system faster and more often than before, allowing companies to use the new technologies instead of waiting years for a hard and difficult system upgrade. To do that, you need to use standard objects. If you have already migrated to S/4, you know what I am talking about needing to adapt the system considering all changes. Using CDS views instead of tables is one step in the clean core approach. 
  • It already speaks Fiori. SAP does the hard work of the joins and associations, so you just use it the way you need, and it's all ready for the day you want an Object Page.

Yes, I know. It's not our language YET, we don't know those CDS names yet, and it's so easy to use a table we know. But remember when VBAK sounded just as weird as I_SalesOrder does now? It stuck because we used it every day. This will stick too, if we choose to start.

Now we have AI to help us speed up our knowledge and search for the right object to select from.  But I always use AI as a co-worker and never as the builder and be sure you add on the prompt to use best practices and use Standard objects whenever possible

So let’s go for it! Creating the CDS on Eclipse…

CDS Code 

@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED //Authorization is not required
@EndUserText.label: 'Demo for ABAP Class' //Just a text
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true //
define view entity ZC_DEMO
 as select from I_SalesOrder
{
     @UI.lineItem:       [{ position: 10, importance: #HIGH }] //The field below will be the first (10) column on the report
     @UI.selectionField: [{ position: 10 }] //The field below will be on the app as a search field
 key SalesOrder,
     @UI.lineItem:       [{ position: 20 }]
     SalesOrderType,
     @UI.lineItem:       [{ position: 30 }]
     SalesOrganization,
     @UI.lineItem:       [{ position: 40 }]
     @UI.selectionField: [{ position: 20 }]
     CreationDate,
     @UI.lineItem:       [{ position: 50, label: 'Created Today' }]
     @ObjectModel.virtualElement: true //The field below will use an virtual Element
     @ObjectModel.virtualElementCalculatedBy: 'ABAP:ZCL_VIRT_DEMO' //This is the Class you use to calculate the field below
     cast( ' ' as abap.char(1) ) as CreatedToday
}
where CreationDate >= dats_add_days( $session.system_date, -30, 'NULL' ) //Just select the last 30 days

UI annotations: how the backend tells the frontend what to draw

The Fiori app doesn’t know anything about our fields. The annotations in the CDS are instructions that travel with the OData service, and Fiori elements reads them to build the screen.

In plain English: the CDS doesn’t only deliver the data, it also sends instructions to the screen the user interacts with: “Hey, look, here is what you show in the table and here is what you show in the filters.” 

 In our code:

  • @UI.lineItem: this field becomes a column in the report.
  • @UI.selectionField: this field becomes a filter in the filter bar at the top.

The position number sets the order: 10 comes first, then 20, and so on.

Note: I prefer using a Metadata Extension (a separate file that keeps the annotations out of the CDS view), but I really want to keep this very simple here.

Step 2: Create the Virtual Class

Note: I know we could get this logic using a CASE in the CDS, but the idea here is to show how to use the class in a very simple example that everybody understand 😉

This part here is important, so let's translate what this part of the code is saying: 

"Hey CDS, this field will use a virtual element. The value will be calculated by an ABAP class called ZCL_VIRT_DEMO. If nothing is returned, the value is blank. The field will contain a value of 1 char (ABAP CHAR1) and will be exposed as CreatedToday. Nice. See you in the class!" 

So now we need to create the virtual class. 

 

The code

CLASS zcl_virt_demo DEFINITION
 PUBLIC                      "Can be used by other objects
 FINAL                       "Cannot be inherited
 CREATE PUBLIC.
 PUBLIC SECTION.
   "This makes the class a calculator for virtual elements
   INTERFACES if_sadl_exit_calc_element_read.
ENDCLASS.
CLASS zcl_virt_demo IMPLEMENTATION.
 "STEP 1 - Runs FIRST, before the database read.
 "Which real fields do you need to calculate your virtual field?"
 METHOD if_sadl_exit_calc_element_read~get_calculation_info.
   "Only if the app really asked for CreatedToday (names come in UPPERCASE)
   IF line_exists( it_requested_calc_elements[ table_line = 'CREATEDTODAY' ] ).
     "Tell SADL to also read CreationDate from the database
     APPEND 'CREATIONDATE' TO et_requested_orig_elements.
   ENDIF.
 ENDMETHOD.
 "STEP 2 - Runs AFTER the database read, once per package of rows.
 "Here we fill the virtual field.
 METHOD if_sadl_exit_calc_element_read~calculate.
   "Table typed with the CDS view, so we can access fields by name
   DATA lt_orders TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF zc_demo WITH DEFAULT KEY.
   "Copy the generic data into our typed table
   lt_orders = CORRESPONDING #( it_original_data ).
   "Read the date once, outside the loop (no need to ask on every row)
   DATA(lv_today) = cl_abap_context_info=>get_system_date( ).
   LOOP AT lt_orders ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<order>).
     "Created today? Mark with 'X'
     IF <order>-creationdate = lv_today.
       <order>-createdtoday = 'X'.
     ENDIF.
   ENDLOOP.
   "Give the result back to SADL (same rows, same order)
   ct_calculated_data = CORRESPONDING #( lt_orders ).
 ENDMETHOD.
ENDCLASS.

How to debug it

Go to SE24 and search for the class you created. 

Double-click the method you want to debug and create an EXTERNAL breakpoint. 

Important

You can preview the data in Eclipse, right? Yes, but there the class will not be called, and the virtual element comes back blank. Don’t do what I did: I thought my class wasn’t working and spent a long time trying to understand why! Let me save you the trouble: to see the class running, you need to create the service definition, the service binding and the app. 

Step 3: Service Definition and Service Binding

Service Definition - You tell the OData service (the object that selects the data) what you want to be displayed in the result. 

The Code

@EndUserText.label: 'Service Definition for ZC_DEMO'
define service ZUI_DEMO {
 expose ZC_DEMO;
}

Service Binding - You expose the service definition as an OData V4 UI service, so the app can consume your CDS data. 

Activate

When it does not activate

Depending on the architecture of your system, you might not be able to publish your service in Eclipse. If this is your case and you are using V4, you need to go to tcode /n/IWFND/V4_ADMIN. 

Search for your Service Binding, select it and publish it. 

Go back to Eclipse and you will see that the binding is now published.

Step 4: Creating a List Report Page

Just leave the project attributes as they are and finish the project.

You will get a message like the one below:

When it finishes, you will get this message:

  • Open Folder means you will only get this project in BAS.
  • Add Project to Workspace means it will be added to your other projects in BAS. I always use this option. 

Then you can preview the application by right clicking on webapp

The terminal will run and another tab will open with your app! Voilá!

Step 5 - Adding a UI5 element on top of the report

 Until here things went smoothly, but I want to add a Radial Micro Chart on top of the report. So my first instinct was to look for the controller and the view, but there was no MVC… WHAT??????? 

But first, what is MVC?

If you don't know what MVC means and you are an ABAPer, please read this blog post:  Getting cozy with familiar ABAP terms on your new BTP neighborhood 

It was a surprise to me, and then I thought: "Wait... does every template have completely different code and a completely different way of developing?" Gosh! 😅 (Actually, I said a bad word, but let's keep this blog civilized.)

But, as I mentioned in my previous blog Overwhelmed by SAP's new everything? Read this before you give up! I moved from being overwhelmed to being curious, and this time I was curious about how I would add the logic in the backend and not in the frontend.

So I asked Claude and, after a long discussion and a lot of changes, we decided that the best option was to create a Basic app because it was more familiar to me (my first 2 apps were created using Basic Template; be aware that to get to those 2 apps I created like 10 hahahaha).

The main point was that it was very simple to achieve parts of this using the List Report Page, but I couldn't make my UI5 element show up in the app using a custom UI5 extension (a controller file I added to the app), which probably says more about me than about the template. If you know the trick, please tell me. And with the Basic Template, I was trying to reinvent the wheel way too hard.

Then I was like: "There is NO WAY no one wanted to do this before and it is this hard!!"

Trust AI but learn your stuff

I started investigating it. I have taken lots and lots of SAP courses over the course of my career, and many were focused on UX, so I knew about the floorplans. Let's be honest here: it's so easy to think that AI knows more than you do! I think this is going to be the learning curve with this tool: understanding that your expertise matters more than you think.

So I learned that there is something called the Analytical List Page (ALP). The ALP is exactly the combination I was after: KPIs on top, report below. EXACTLY what I need. Claude never suggested it to me until I suggested it to Claude, and then it said that it was obvious that ALP was the best option 😅

What did I learn from this project? 

The nicest thing about being new at something is that once you overcome the first aversion to the new, you learn a lot very fast and mostly by making mistakes. With this project I tried a custom UI5 extension, two new floorplans, an ABAP class in a CDS, an analytical data definition and more.

Now I know when to use an Analytical List Page and when to use a List Report Page. List Report when the goal is to list and filter. ALP when you want KPIs and charts on top, working together with the list below. 

I tried to summarize it all here so you could learn from my experience. Let me know if it worked! 😉

——————

While this post might be basic to some, I added here everything that was getting me overwhelmed for years and all my questions related to those things. My goal with these posts is to demystify the new SAP development world together with you.

I'll continue sharing simple posts based on real discoveries, real questions and real experiences, sharing my journey, my learnings and my bumps along the way so you don't need to go through some of them yourself.

If you're in the same boat, stay tuned. There will be many more posts about this journey.

If you're further along than this, pretty please help us in the comments.

To be continued

I’m on holiday now, in Brazil to be more exact , so there’s no ALP update yet (yes, I’m still writing here, apparently I can’t help it 😅). But I will write about the Analytical List Page as soon as I’m back and get it sorted. And I promise to tell you honestly what worked and what didn’t. 

Thanks for reading!

entry.title: Consuming SAP Integration Suite OData Provisioning from SAP Business Application Studio Across BTP
entry.content:
SAP OData Provisioning with BAS / SAP Fiori Tools Across BTP Subaccounts

Step 1: Configure the Backend Connection for OData Provisioning

In the SAP Integration Suite subaccount, create an HTTP destination pointing to the SAP Business Suite backend.

A simplified destination configuration is:

Name: ECC_ODP_BACKEND

Type: HTTP

ProxyType: OnPremise

Authentication: PrincipalPropagation

sap-client: 100

odc: true

Backend URL: SAP Backend Example

The important OData Provisioning property is:

odc = true

This destination provides the connection from OData Provisioning to the on-premise SAP backend.

Step 2: Register the OData Service

In SAP Integration Suite, navigate to:

Configure

→ OData Services

→ Register

Select the backend destination created in Step 1.

Then register the required OData service.

For example:

ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV

After registration, the service is published through OData Provisioning rather than being consumed directly from the on-premise SAP Gateway endpoint.

Step 3: Create OData Provisioning Runtime Access

For runtime access, create the appropriate OData Provisioning runtime service instance and service key.

The generated credentials conceptually contain the following information:

API URL:

ODP Runtime Host.<region>.hana.ondemand.com

Client ID:

sb-dummy-client-id

Client Secret:

dummy-client-secret

Grant Type:

client_credentials

Token URL:

Authentication Host.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/oauth/token

The configuration discussed here uses:

Service: xfs-runtime

Plan: odpruntime

The service-key credentials provide the information needed to authenticate against the OData Provisioning runtime.

Step 4: Test OAuth Independently from BAS

Before configuring SAP Fiori Tools, first verify the ODP runtime independently from the BAS terminal.

Obtain an OAuth access token using the Client ID and Client Secret.

Example command:

curl -s \

-X POST \

-u 'sb-dummy-client-id:dummy-client-secret' \

-H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \

-d 'grant_type=client_credentials' \

'ODP OAuth Token Endpoint'

After receiving the token, save it locally:

export TOKEN='<access-token>'

This test is useful because it validates OAuth authentication separately from the SAP Fiori Tools configuration.

Step 5: Use the Correct ODP Runtime Endpoint

This was one of the key findings during troubleshooting.

Initially, the Integration Suite application URL was tested using a URL similar to:

https://<tenant>.integrationsuite.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/xfsrt/odp/...

An unauthenticated curl request returned:

HTTP 200

However, the returned content was:

Content-Type: text/html

The response contained an interactive XSUAA login flow rather than an OData response.

Therefore, an important troubleshooting rule is:

HTTP 200 does not automatically mean that the OData request succeeded.

The correct test in this setup is against the ODP runtime host supplied by the runtime credentials.

Example:

ODP Runtime Endpoint

Step 6: Validate an Individual OData Service

The working ODP service URL follows this structure:

https://services.odp.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/odata/SAP/<SERVICE>;v=<VERSION>/

For example:

ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV

To retrieve the service metadata, execute:

curl -sk \

-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \

-H "Accept: application/xml" \

"ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV Metadata"

A successful result should return:

HTTP 200 OK

and:

Content-Type: application/xml

The metadata should begin with an XML element similar to:

<edmx:Edmx ...>

At this stage, the test independently validates:

  • BAS network connectivity: OK
  • OAuth token acquisition: OK
  • ODP runtime authentication: OK
  • Registered OData service: OK
  • OData metadata retrieval: OK

Step 7: Validate the OData Provisioning Service Catalog

Another important finding is that OData Provisioning exposes its own CATALOGSERVICE.

The catalog metadata can be tested using:

curl -sk \

-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \

-H "Accept: application/xml" \

"https://services.odp.cfapps.eu10.hana.ondemand.com/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2/$metadata"

The catalog contains entities such as:

  • ServiceCollection
  • CatalogCollection
  • Annotations
  • Vocabularies
  • TagCollection
  • EntitySetCollection

To retrieve the registered OData services:

curl -sk \

-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \

-H "Accept: application/json" \

'ODP Service Collection'

For a registered service such as ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV, the response contains information conceptually similar to:

Description: Project Request

Title: ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV

TechnicalServiceName: ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV

TechnicalServiceVersion: 1

Service URL: ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV

Metadata URL: ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV Metadata

This proves independently that the ODP catalog itself is working correctly.

Step 8: Configure the BAS / Build Code Subaccount Destination

In the BAS / Build Code subaccount, create the following destination.

Name: SAP_Gateway

Type: HTTP

URL: ODP Runtime Host

ProxyType: Internet

Authentication: OAuth2ClientCredentials

Client ID: sb-dummy-client-id

Client Secret: dummy-client-secret

Token Service URL: ODP OAuth Token Endpoint

Add the following additional properties:

WebIDEEnabled: true

WebIDEUsage: odata_gen

HTML5.DynamicDestination: true

HTML5.Timeout: 60000

Important

Do not add $metadata to the destination URL.

The destination should point to the ODP runtime host.

Understanding WebIDEUsage

Understanding WebIDEUsage became one of the most important parts of the troubleshooting.

WebIDEUsage = odata_gen

With:

WebIDEUsage = odata_gen

SAP Fiori Tools treats the destination as a generic/partial OData destination in the tested setup.

In the Fiori Application Generator, select:

Connect to a System

→ SAP_Gateway

BAS then presents a Service Path field.

Enter the required ODP service path.

For example:

/odata/SAP/ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV;v=1/

This works in the tested environment.

The configuration is therefore effectively:

ODP Runtime Host

  •  

OData Service Path

=

Complete OData Service URL

For example:

ODP Runtime Host:

services.odp.cfapps.eu10.hana.ondemand.com

Service Path:

/odata/SAP/ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV;v=1/

Why odata_abap Fails with OData Provisioning

Initially, the expectation was that:

WebIDEUsage = odata_abap

would allow BAS / SAP Fiori Tools to display and browse the ODP catalog automatically.

Instead, BAS returned:

Internal server error

Request failed with status code 500

Running:

Fiori: Open Environment Check

revealed the actual problem.

For OData V2 catalog discovery, Fiori Tools constructed:

/sap/opu/odata/IWFND/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

For OData V4, it attempted:

/sap/opu/odata4/iwfnd/config/default/iwfnd/catalog/0002

These are ABAP Gateway catalog routes.

However, the working OData Provisioning catalog in this environment is:

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

Therefore, there is a catalog-path mismatch.

OData Provisioning

Catalog Path:

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

Result: OK

BAS with odata_abap

Catalog Path attempted by Fiori Tools:

/sap/opu/odata/IWFND/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

Result: FAIL

This means the observed issue was not caused by OAuth authentication.

It was not caused by Cloud Connector connectivity.

It was not caused by ODP service registration.

It was not caused by the ODP runtime itself.

The problem was the difference between the catalog URL exposed by OData Provisioning and the standard ABAP Gateway catalog URL expected by the odata_abap discovery flow.

What About odata_hcp_odp?

Older SAP Web IDE documentation contains another WebIDEUsage value:

WebIDEUsage = odata_hcp_odp

Historically, the distinction was:

odata_abap

for OData services hosted on SAP Gateway systems.

Whereas:

odata_hcp_odp

was associated with OData Provisioning systems on SAP Cloud Platform.

This initially appeared to match the required architecture.

However, in the tested current BAS/Fiori Tools environment, after configuring:

WebIDEUsage = odata_hcp_odp

the destination was not displayed in the Fiori Application Generator.

The observed behavior was therefore:

odata_gen

Destination visible

→ Service Path field available

→ ODP service path can be entered

→ Works

odata_abap

Destination visible

→ Standard ABAP catalog attempted

→ Catalog discovery fails

odata_hcp_odp

Destination not displayed in the tested Fiori Application Generator

Current Working Approach

For the tested BAS/Fiori Tools environment, the reliable configuration was:

URL: services.odp.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com

Authentication: OAuth2ClientCredentials

WebIDEUsage: odata_gen

WebIDEEnabled: true

HTML5.DynamicDestination: true

HTML5.Timeout: 60000

Developers then select:

Connect to a System

↓

SAP_Gateway

↓

Service Path

and enter:

/odata/SAP/<SERVICE>;v=<VERSION>/

For example:

/odata/SAP/ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV;v=1/

Catalog Browsing Limitation

The ODP catalog itself is operational.

The registered services can be retrieved from:

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2/ServiceCollection

However, in the tested BAS/Fiori Tools environment, the native Connect to a System → catalog selection flow could not consume the ODP catalog in the same way.

The important distinction is:

OData Provisioning Flow

ODP

↓

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

↓

Direct OAuth request works

↓

ServiceCollection

↓

ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV

BAS odata_abap Flow

BAS / Fiori Tools

↓

WebIDEUsage = odata_abap

↓

/sap/opu/odata/IWFND/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

↓

Fails because a different catalog path is being requested

If the catalog-selection UX is mandatory, support for an ODP-specific discovery mechanism should be validated for the target SAP Fiori Tools environment.

Principal Propagation and End-User Identity

There is another important distinction between design-time authentication and runtime end-user identity propagation.

OAuth2ClientCredentials is useful in this scenario for:

  • Design-time connectivity
  • Verifying the ODP runtime
  • Retrieving the ODP catalog
  • Retrieving OData metadata
  • Testing the OData service from BAS

However, Client Credentials represents the OAuth client, not the interactive Fiori end user.

If the runtime requirement is:

User A logs into Fiori

↓

Request reaches ABAP

↓

sy-uname = USER_A

and:

User B logs into Fiori

↓

Request reaches ABAP

↓

sy-uname = USER_B

then the runtime architecture must preserve the user context rather than relying solely on the Client Credentials token.

In the described landscape, the downstream configuration was:

OData Provisioning

↓

Principal Propagation Destination

↓

SAP Cloud Connector

↓

ABAP Backend

When accessed using the required interactive user context, the mapped SAP user was received in the ABAP backend through:

sy-uname

Therefore, BAS design-time authentication and runtime end-user principal propagation should be treated as separate concerns.

Troubleshooting Checklist

1. Check Network Connectivity

Verify that BAS can reach the ODP runtime host:

services.odp.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com

If this fails, troubleshoot network connectivity before investigating the Fiori Tools configuration.

2. Check OAuth Authentication

Verify that the ODP runtime service credentials can generate an OAuth access token.

Confirm that the following are correct:

  • Client ID
  • Client Secret
  • Grant Type
  • Token Service URL

The expected grant type in this setup is:

client_credentials

3. Check the Individual ODP Service

Using the OAuth token, retrieve:

/odata/SAP/<SERVICE>;v=<VERSION>/$metadata

For example:

/odata/SAP/ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV;v=1/$metadata

A successful response should return:

HTTP 200 OK

and XML metadata.

4. Check the ODP Catalog

Using the same OAuth token, verify:

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2/$metadata

Then verify:

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2/ServiceCollection?$format=json

If both requests succeed, the ODP catalog itself is operational.

5. Run BAS Environment Check

In BAS, run:

Fiori: Open Environment Check

This was particularly useful because it exposed the catalog URL that Fiori Tools was actually requesting.

In this case, it showed:

/sap/opu/odata/IWFND/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

rather than the working ODP catalog path:

/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2

6. Always Inspect the Response Content Type

A common troubleshooting mistake is assuming:

HTTP 200 = OData request succeeded

That is not necessarily true.

For $metadata, expect an XML response such as:

Content-Type: application/xml

The response should contain metadata beginning with something similar to:

<edmx:Edmx>

If the response instead contains:

Content-Type: text/html

the request may have returned an authentication or login page rather than OData metadata.

Final Validation Result

The tested setup produced the following results:

✅ BAS → ODP network connectivity: WORKING

✅ ODP OAuth runtime access: WORKING

✅ ODP service metadata: WORKING

✅ ODP CATALOGSERVICE: WORKING

✅ ODP ServiceCollection: WORKING

✅ ODP → ABAP Principal Propagation: WORKING

✅ odata_gen + Service Path: WORKING

❌ odata_abap automatic catalog browsing: NOT WORKING

⚠️ Historical odata_hcp_odp: Destination not displayed in the tested current Fiori Application Generator

Conclusion

The most important lesson from this troubleshooting exercise is to separate four different layers:

1. BAS → ODP Network Connectivity

2. BAS → ODP Authentication

3. Fiori Tools Design-Time Service Discovery

4. ODP → SAP Backend Principal Propagation

In this case, network connectivity worked.

OAuth runtime authentication worked.

Individual OData service metadata worked.

The ODP CATALOGSERVICE worked.

The ODP ServiceCollection worked.

Principal Propagation from ODP to the ABAP backend worked.

The remaining problem was specifically the design-time catalog-discovery mechanism used by Fiori Tools with odata_abap.

The working development approach in the tested environment was therefore:

SAP Integration Suite

↓

OData Provisioning

↓

xfs-runtime OAuth Credentials

↓

BAS Destination

↓

WebIDEUsage = odata_gen

↓

Connect to a System

↓

SAP_Gateway

↓

Service Path

↓

/odata/SAP/<SERVICE>;v=<VERSION>/

For example:

/odata/SAP/ZPROJECT_REQUEST_SRV;v=1/

This approach keeps the SAP Integration Suite OData Provisioning runtime separate from the underlying SAP Gateway implementation and provides the working path used in this cross-subaccount setup.
